description: Alexander the Great cultivated an ideal of Homeric heroism, consciously modeling himself on figures such as Achilles and treating personal courage as essential to kingship. He frequently fought near the front, accepted extraordinary physical risks, and sought glory through conspicuous acts of bravery, reflecting an aristocratic belief that a ruler should prove his worth through action as well as command. His admiration for Homer, especially the Iliad, shaped a personal philosophy centered on arete—excellence, honor, ambition, and the pursuit of lasting fame—so that conquest became not merely political expansion, but a stage on which Alexander could emulate the heroic warriors of Greece’s legendary past.
